Neuromorphic systems hold promise for enhancing computing throughput and energy efficiency; nonetheless, emerging neuromorphic accelerators depend on extensive simulations utilizing extensive and intricate microarchitectures. To manage such a complex design and large-scale simulation environment, it is essential to employ a neucro-morphic simulation framework capable of parallelizing massive workloads effectively. In addition, reducing the memory footprint and enhancing both speed and scalability are critical for efficient execution. This study introduces a modular, multi-level architecture for a virtual platform designed to facilitate large-scale simulations with reduced memory consumption. We evaluate various virtual platform segmentation schemes and compare their impact on simulation performance. Furthermore, we parallelize this multi-tier architectural approach, enabling large-scale simulations. Our results demonstrate that parallelizing a segmentation strategy based on task graph cuts memory use by 90% while achieving a 32x speed increase; this method supports a 32-core, large, complex simulation that was previously unattainable, or at least infeasible, with other simulation strategies for this machine.

Traditional "if-then" rules are often inadequate for the intricate, ill-defined nature of the world, whether in human decision-making or agent design, necessitating a more robust inferential framework. While "decision trees" (DT) have long served as a popular alternative by modeling logical implications to support belief updates, "Indecision Trees" (IDT) have emerged as an extension capable of handling uncertainty without linearizing information excessively. Preserving non-linear data representations is vital for meaningful world modeling, making the ability to do so a key advantage. Since the advent of "Neural Indecision Trees" (NIDT), which unify classic IDT structures with continuous function learning capabilities, their potential has been highlighted. However, existing solutions often neglect efficient training protocols, rendering current methods computationally slow and unsuitable for real-time applications like autonomous driving or robotics. To address this, the paper presents a sample-based training methodology that is both simple and effective. Demonstrations across six benchmark datasets show this approach significantly outperforms linearized variants and legacy tree structures in area under curve (AUC) scores, all while maintaining rapid, real-time inference speed.

This study examines the performance enhancement of single-pass techniques for time series similarity search through the premature termination of the comparison process. Multiple models were evaluated, with the best results achieved using a non-linear approach based on the first-order difference of a series combined with $L_2$ distance. Evaluation on five datasets revealed that single-pass Early Abandoning outperformed traditional post-hoc versions by a significant margin.

Automated code completion tools are rapidly transforming how individuals learn to code, yet research into their efficacy during the educational setting remains scarce. To address this gap, we conducted a large-scale educational study featuring 1,571 first-year computer science students, analyzing their interaction logs with a specific automated code completion system. We evaluated three distinct intervention conditions: providing students with real-time, immediate feedback on their own code, offering them periodic weekly summaries of performance metrics instead, or allowing them to complete tasks with no system feedback. Additionally, we varied the underlying natural language processing components of the assistance provided. Our analysis revealed that access to immediate feedback resulted in higher code coverage and improved programming scores, although students producing code with better overall readability tended to struggle when generating more comprehensive code coverage. Furthermore, the benefits derived from these interventions were independent of which version of the completion system (characterized by differing NLP components) the students utilized. To support researchers in designing more effective in-class assistance, this paper also introduces a comprehensive set of novel metrics for assessing both student interactions with and the pedagogical utility of automated code completion systems.

Black-box classifiers are frequently employed in practice, yet they pose challenges to users due to their lack of comprehensibility. While existing methods for explaining these models rely on identifying patterns in the trained classifier, an alternative approach involves constructing symbolic surrogate models that elucidate a black-box classifier by identifying and leveraging patterns from untrained input-data pairs and outcomes. Previous efforts yielding black-box explanatory models utilize non-hierarchical, black-box algorithms that complicate the interpretation of the resulting symbol-based surrogates. This paper presents a technique for discovering hierarchical symbolic surrogate models (BSMS) by employing an advanced genetic programming method called SOGA. This approach exploits the syntax and semantics of the resulting program to generate hierarchical structures. Our experiments demonstrate that SOGA produces syntactically legible models explaining the black-box algorithms at a level of comprehension equal or superior to those generated by other model production methods.

Understanding the roots of representational limitations is a crucial, yet underexplored, area for accelerating graph machine learning. This study focuses on over-smoothing in Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) as a primary driver of such limitations. We begin by demonstrating that standard GCNs possess an implicit limit on the number of layers because they fail to reach a steady state, consequently causing the quality of node representations to deteriorate. Subsequently, examining recent approaches from a theoretical perspective, we show that over-writing the adjacency matrix with its normalized version fails to resolve implicit over-smoothing. Our analysis further reveals a specific class of Graph GCNs for which over-smoothing is unavoidable; in these cases, the network effectively acts as an low-pass filter, with its bandwidth constrained by architectural choices and graph-specific traits. The proposed contribution presents Theorem 1 and associated algorithms that analyze GCNs through a spectral lens. This framework facilitates the identification of over-smoothing phenomena and guides the design of deeper architectures capable of capturing a wider spectrum of graph signals. Empirical validations using empirical datasets and synthetic data sets confirm the practical utility of this proposed methodological framework.

Employing transmission electron microscopy (TEM), we elucidated critical factors for obtaining monodomain hexagonal $6H\text{-}SiC$ single crystals via epitaxial growth on graphene substrates. The study identified growth temperature as a decisive variable, as it determines the competitive formation of six distinct crystalline domains. While low temperatures favor the parallel selection of closely related rotational variants within the $\{4\bar{}\ 4\ 1\}$ orientation, high-temperature conditions promote a single, unique epitaxial relationship. Furthermore, the formation of these domains is initiated by carbon-rich nanostructures of atomic scale derived from the graphene substrate. The final observed hexagonal symmetry results from the competitive selection among these competing domains during crystal expansion, effectively masking any underlying cubic symmetry that might exist in the as-grown film. The proposed model also offers insights into similar phenomena previously reported in $6H\text{-}SiC$ epitaxy using other substrates.

Common trends are shared stochastic trends embedded within a system's dynamics, and failing to account for common factors can lead to inconsistent forecasts and biased analyses in multivariate time series. Consequently, a crucial initial step in common time series modeling involves detecting these factors, as existing techniques, which rely on strict assumptions of finite variance, often break down with heavy-tailed data. This study introduces a novel, intuitive, and computationally efficient estimator for the number of common trends that is both robust to the magnitude of variance and adaptive to the tail behavior of the data. Under reasonable assumptions, the estimator is consistent, converging in probability to the true common trend count, with a simple limit formula. Furthermore, based on both common trends and arbitrary linear transformations of the data, the authors develop test statistics that are consistent under the stationary null hypothesis, a finding supported by rigorous proofs. Extensive simulations demonstrate the proposed estimator's accuracy and precision, while real-world analyses, including studies on U.S. macroeconomic and financial time series, reveal heavy tails in the residuals of univariate GARCH models. These realizations indicate that post-transforming the data to remove mean and trends, or other heavy tail features, prior to subsequent multi-series analyses yields improved models.

Galaxy clusters serve as massive cosmic lenses, distorting the images of galaxies behind them. Historically, the shapes and positions of these background sources were analyzed independently of the cluster's foreground mass distribution. However, in recent times, the rise of high-resolution imaging has revealed that clusters harbor numerous small perturbers, including numerous stars from merging clusters and a dense population of globular clusters. These stars, despite their individual tiny gravitational impacts, collectively introduce noise into lensing measurements. We develop a novel approach to quantify the specific contribution of such small perturbers to these lensing systematics. By combining a non-linear fast multipole method with a three-dimensional model of galaxy clusters based on $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, we demonstrate that these systematics peak in the cores of clusters and can reach amplitudes of $\sim10^{-4}$. This effect is most pronounced in systems with high central mass concentrations and a high density of stars. We propose that upcoming data from the Euclid mission should account for the anticipated $10^{-4}$ level of contributions from stars and globular clusters when analyzing the cores of these clusters. Furthermore, we suggest that utilizing the outer regions of the systems, where these effects diminish to negligible levels below $10^{-5}$, offers the most effective path for precisely estimating the impacts of individual stars.

Non-credible second-price auctions often yield zero revenue for sellers, failing to even generate maximum potential revenue despite sellers violating their own guidelines. This paper posits that sellers neglect revenue collection because complying with their own rules conflicts with the behavioral insights derived from break-the-bank experiments, specifically regarding consumers' unwillingness to forgo winning items entirely for marginal price increases. Certain tasks in computer vision, specifically those like Visual Relationship Detection, face challenges in optimizing their architectural models due to severe class imbalance during the training data labeling process. These inconsistencies between class frequencies can distort the model's focus, particularly in scenarios where negative examples vastly outnumber positive ones, causing optimization algorithms to become biased toward the dominant positive classes. Although recent methods have attempted to address this imbalance, most existing approaches suffer from inefficiency or inaccurate estimation of negative samples. Consequently, this study introduces a Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS) strategy designed to resolve these issues by ensuring model adaptation focuses more equally on both positive and negative inputs during training. BNPS operates in two phases: first, it constructs balanced pairs of positive and negative candidates through a straightforward filtering technique; second, it employs an innovative weighting scheme to dynamically adjust the significance of negative pairs based on their true labels. Experimental results indicate that BNPS effectively enhances the efficiency of the training optimization process while also providing a precise estimation of negative instances via its balancing mechanism.

Neural network template designs frequently leverage grouping nodes by feature channels to create flexible, feed-forward architectures; however, static templates often mandate the presence of all nodes regardless of a specific task's requirements. This over-allocation leads to excessive memory usage and elevated computational complexity. We introduce a method for adaptively sampling nodes from these templates during both training and inference based on confidence scores, thereby creating channel-aware, sparse subgraphs. This adaptable feature set results in customized architectures that maintain accuracy while significantly boosting computational efficiency. Our proposed node sampling strategy is particularly well-suited to hardware with asynchronous support, such as TPUs. Additionally, we present an optimization technique that pre-optimizes the proposed sampling process for streamlined, accelerated inference on standard accelerators equipped with channel grouping.

Leveraging the detailed spectral information from these images, we refine the standard pixel-level annotation process by defining labels based on material instances rather than individual pixels. To date, there hasn't been a systematic study examining how frequently global policymakers express interest in specific areas of science related to climate change. Research in dialogue systems has historically focused on enhancing conversation quality through the refinement of architectural models and the application of vast datasets. Langevin dynamics is a prevalent framework for simulating biomolecules and materials science systems; however, most implementations rely on a constant temperature, limiting its use in scenarios where temperature varies spatially. This study introduces and investigates an extension of Einstein relativity—adapting it for spatially dependent thermal baths. We validate this approach by adapting the extended reaction coordinate block algorithm (RCE), demonstrating through control problems that simulations run efficiently across both constant and spatially dependent temperatures. Furthermore, we analyze current ratchets to Lennanize dynamics solutions and confirm that they also yield correct results under spatial temperature variations.

This study introduces a straightforward method to derive a lower bound on the over-the-air message-passing (OMP) capacity of LDPC codes featuring negative degree-correlation among their structures. Its practical method overcomes a primary difficulty in prior attempts—a requirement for calculating intractable integrals—by providing an accessible estimate of these challenging integrals. Empirical results demonstrate that this derived bound is notably closer to the actual OMP capacities generated by such codes. Furthermore, this bound effectively predicts the maximum sustainable erasure probability (the critical erasure threshold) for these codes. Finally, we prove that negative degree-correlation within LDPC ensembles yields higher critical erasure bounds compared to randomly constructed ensembles.

This research investigates the input-to-state stability (ISS) of multiple support point forward (MPSF) schemes designed for rigid-body walking robots operating under bounded disturbances. Although Rigid Body Dynamics (RBD)—the mathematical framework employed by these schemes to compute foot trajectories and regulatory forces during collision—is a nonlinear system, the MPSF formulation simplifies constraints and calculations by adopting linear approximations. Building on this computational strategy, we propose the ISS multiple-point MPSF (SL-MPSF) scheme, a method to maintain system safety within a positively invariant set for linear systems. Unlike the original nonlinear formulation, SL-MPF employs an extended invariant set and a linear control strategy, thereby enhancing computational efficiency and simplifying the regulatory process. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the ISS multiple-point MPSF guarantees stability for the resulting closed-loop nonlinear system generated by combining the MPSF-generated forces with the robot's dynamics. Finally, simulations utilizing a bi-cycloid gauged gait confirm that the SL-MPF effectively enlarges the allowable disturbance region compared to its nonlinear counterpart.

Current vacuum and weak-decoy-state quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols remain highly efficient for generating secret keys at commercial scale, leading to their extensive deployment. Despite this practical success, large-scale weak-decoy-state QKD systems have never been empirically validated for security against realistic attacker models, due to difficulty in conceiving specific attacks that satisfy strict detection criteria. We present and experimentally verify the world's first phishing attack on such a system in an all-optical fashion. In this attack, an adversary (Eve) exploits the inertness of single-photon components within the user (Alice)'s equipment. The process begins with the substitution of vacuum states sent by the legitimate Alice with those prepared at an interception point, ensuring no losses and thus no detection by the Alice-Bob link without any physical modification of the transmission channel. Without altering other parameters, Eve substitutes photons from weak decoys with strong ones; this increases interference detection rates on Bob's side, allowing the estimation of side-channel information even if rate errors exist. This technique provides the interception side with access upper bounds significantly more generous than those available through standard attacks. The phishing protocol is exclusively optical, circumventing the need for quantum-memory storage. Introducing this novel side-channel opens up new research avenues in quantum cryptography and underscores a critical design principle: the security of QKD systems is contingent not just on input parameters, but on internal architectural specifics.

Recent observational findings regarding $CPT$ violation in beauty baryons and the charm system significantly advance our grasp of charm physics, alongside the scarce but notable results concerning $CPT$ violation within top quarks. These findings demand an urgent theoretical investigation into the underlying physics, prompting theoretical models that explain the observed $CPT$ violation alongside proposals for experimental verification through future colliders. However, the theoretical framework interpreting these specific results under the constraint of CPT theorem remains constrained by extreme scarcity. This abstract therefore presents a preliminary study aimed at constructing the first phenomenological interpretation for these signals within an expanded version of the Standard Model, specifically targeting instanton-induced $CPT$ violation as the foundational cause. In our proposed scenario, we demonstrate consistency with the experimental data while maintaining gauge anomaly cancellation. Furthermore, our work provides novel theoretical insight: we reveal that the phase associated with instanton-induced $CPT$ violation is inherently linked to the conventional strong $CP$ parameter, implying a potential connection between the observed signals and the solution for resolving the strong $CP$ problem.

This article addresses energy cost optimization for edge computing infrastructure by employing a Markov decision process (MDP) framework. We propose two enhancement techniques: (1) a neural optimizer that automatically learns policy parameters and (2) parameter sharing, which distributes computing capabilities across multiple edge nodes to reduce local neural network sizes. Additionally, we define a rigorous performance evaluation metric to distinguish the efficacy of different policy strategies. Simulation results confirm that both proposed approaches significantly lower energy costs, demonstrating the potential for widespread adoption in practical edge deployments and facilitating scalable solutions through edge computation.

Existing speech synthesis frameworks treat the clustering of transient speech segments as undesirable noise rather than an intrinsic characteristic, resulting in noisy training data and biased models. This study examines speech synthesis from the standpoint of clustering transient and steady-state regions. We propose a novel training objective designed to separate these regions during training alongside a technique for their individual separate training. Furthermore, by applying cluster-specific control parameters for transients and steady-states, we can precisely regulate their frequency within synthesized outputs. Our proposed method demonstrates improved objective and subjective quality over baseline approaches, yielding significant enhancements in the correctness of transcriptions and perceived naturalness regarding synthesized audio.

This study introduces a multi-stage optimization framework designed for online motion planning of free-floating space walkers. The approach optimizes trajectories for a fully actuated two-degree-of-freedom spacecraft coupled with a simplified three-degree-of-freedom manipulator. By decomposing the complex problem into four distinct optimization steps, the method enhances computational speed and planning efficiency. The first stage addresses spacecraft attitude reconfiguration to optimally realign the spacecraft's center of mass relative to the attached walker. Subsequent stages involve: (2) calculating a coarse trajectory for the manipulator based on the prior results; (3) refining the motion plan using the coarse trajectory as initialization; and (4) executing an final computation on embedded hardware. Validation through simulations based on a space-based astronomical observation scenario demonstrates that this multi-tiered strategy significantly reduces computation time, satisfying real-time requirements for implementation.

This study presents a technique for resolving polynomial linear systems that minimizes the count required for solution discovery in the presence of noise. Subsequently, performance metrics regarding the method are assessed, demonstrating that it successfully generates reliable position reconstructions necessary for future research on the JUNO experiment.

This study introduces a novel approach for characterizing and optimizing Atmospheric Data Communications (ADC) systems operating in the optical domain. The proposed framework leverages Fast Optical Vector Signals (FOVS) combined with Monte Carlo (MC) techniques, enabling the simultaneous evaluation of channel bit errors (BE) and Optical Signal-to-Noise Ratios (OSNR) alongside the effective propagation matrix. By merging these elements, the new methodology provides comprehensive insights into the atmospheric channel properties. Furthermore, it enables the derivation of crucial design metrics, including the optimum eye safety index (OESI)—defined as maximizing information transmission prior to reaching a specified optical power threshold—and the optimal eye safety filter (OESF). Crucially, only first-order statistics of light intensity fluctuations are required for these calculations. The findings indicate that while standard atmospheric propagation models, specifically the Log-Normal model used in most existing literature for beam divergence estimation across various wavelengths, should generally be discarded in ADC applications (particularly in the blue spectrum) to ensure precise ADC designs. Instead, robust experimental techniques paired with straightforward MC simulations constitute superior alternatives. Ultimately, the paper presents a standardized, replicable procedure for calculating OESF that operates independent of specific atmospheric conditions.

This study introduces PILE, a novel, computationally efficient method designed specifically for unsupervised scene segmentation. Unlike traditional iterative co-training approaches that rely on full-scale label data, PILE synthesizes reliable supervisory signals during training by estimating reliable confidence levels based exclusively on pair-wise comparisons between segmentation outputs of two different neural networks. Empirically evaluated against two unsupervised scenarios, PILE demonstrated efficient execution and achieved segmentation accuracy that substantially surpasses current state-of-the-art methodologies in quality.

Ultralight bosonic dark matter interacting with nucleons may induce ultra-rare, ultra-low-frequency variations in its weak interaction cross-section, which an array of sensors could theoretically detect. This text suggests that even if a single sensor fails to reach the sensitivity needed to observe these signals, the network's ability to measure the exact time of such events allows it to integrate data across the whole system. Consequently, this multi-detector approach enhances the signal's detectability beyond individual limits. This effect is analogous to existing techniques for discovering ultralight dark matter in nuclear transition bands and represents a significant advantage for future experiments targeting signals within a broad spectrum of frequencies. To demonstrate, we apply this method to two existing systems, the Cryogenic Neutral Gas Xenon experiment and Germanium Germanium Array, showing individually they are signal-deficient, but combined, they can potentially detect such intensity variations. This technique is universally general, working regardless of the specific physical mechanism underlying the bosonic dark matter phenomenon.

The findings apply broadly, covering scenarios including generic matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A}$ composed of a known kernel and a known range component. These insights offer fresh insights into the topological structure of the solution set within the basis pursuit framework.

Machine Learning (FL) models, being increasingly integral to our everyday existence, have generated significant moral and ethical concerns. Three prominent approaches for mitigating these issues are fairness metrics, federated training methods, and differential privacy (DP). In this specific scenario, we introduce an elegant DP-based mechanism to produce fairness metrics by analyzing the outcomes of a trained FL system. Continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods represent a class of algorithms featuring a finite number of exponential evaluations per time step at continuously varying points; although introduced over a century ago, their application has been limited due to the typical inefficiency of discretizing integrals arising from time-dependent Hamiltonian systems. This connection facilitates the investigation of computational accuracy, with numerical demonstrations confirming that, although not initially apparent from theoretical formulations, significant precision gains are indeed observed.

We propose a low-energy photon collider framework capable of probing the muon g-2 anomaly parameter space via the $e^+e^-$ fusion channel for $\mu^+\mu^+$ production at a BNL jet facility. The suggested collider design supports both a 50/250 Gene configuration and a dual 250/250 Gene setup, both offering significant sensitivity to resolving the persistent muon g-2 discrepancy. This sensitivity remains robust even in the presence of existing Higgs and top quark precision measurements conducted at the proposed International Linear Collider (ILC). Additionally, we examine the implications of lepton universality violation through the $e^+$ reaction for further testing new physics models.

Human Video Understanding involves addressing complex cognitive tasks where models must integrate visual data across multiple frames to derive semantic context for the entire sequence. Addressing key challenges within video content remains critical for achieving comprehensive scene comprehension, a hurdle traditional models often face due to their focus on temporal flow at the expense of spatial details. To overcome this limitation, we introduce HAN (Hierarchical Attention Network), a dual-branch architecture designed to jointly exploit temporal and spatial correlations across frames. The bottom-up multiple step spatial temporal attention (MS-ST-Net) branch identifies and localizes significant regions within the video sequences. Simultaneously, the bottom-up bottom-right (BS-Net) branch exploits temporal correlations using bidirectional Long-Short Term Memory (LSTMs) across video frames. An innovative hierarchy of Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) integrated with bidirectional capabilities is employed here to capture dynamic temporal evolution. Anamorphic guidance from deep model predictions is utilized to refine model performance, ensuring predictions align accurately with human visual perception and ensuring significant regions are highlighted effectively. Evaluation on the Visual Question Answering (VQA) task demonstrates that HAN surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed architecture is built with bidirectional branch that can highlight significant regions in videos and extract dynamic temporal evolution using a novel hierarchy of Long Short Term Memory. We argue that this observed dependence of outcome on the scattering details implies a specific dependence of the resulting state on those details as well; had black hole final states been determined independently of the scattering process, near-extremal and extremal outcomes would be universally separated into distinct, disjoint sets, an implication our results disprove to determine false therefore. Extending this reasoning to holographic models, we propose a scenario wherein unitary quantum evolution dictates the final state yet remains compatible with both holography and information preservation in unitary quantum evolution.

Symbolic programming languages like Python facilitate the computation of entropies and mutual informations, whether discrete or continuous, by leveraging the ability to evaluate probability distributions directly. However, a significant challenge emerges when these probabilities cannot be computed in their functional form: one must rely on samples drawn from the underlying distributions. This study introduces a Monte Carlo framework for calculating such measures in the absence of analytical evaluation. Notably, our methodology addresses complex, analytical expressions involving variables x and y that involve multivariate integrals, by representing the target distribution as a combination of sampleable components. Thus, even when a joint distribution cannot be explicitly assessed, it can often be reconstructed through sampling from simpler constituent parts.

Building upon prior findings that represent states as Borel measures and define net fluxes as absolutely continuous measures relative to the underlying state, the authors introduce additional characterizations for these properties. Furthermore, the article identifies sufficient conditions requiring a state to belong to a set defined by constraints on fluxes between specific subsystems, addressing both discrete and group-based resource models while concluding with an exploration of state convergence toward a Borel-measurable limit.

Network intrusion detection is vital for identifying and neutralizing active threats, yet keeping such systems up-to-date with new attack signatures is difficult due to the continuous evolution of attack types and the consequent need for frequent classifier updates. Simultaneously, many Internet of Things (IoT) devices operate with severe limitations on power, memory, and processing capacity, making these complex systems unfeasible to run directly on such hardware. Distributed intrusion detection offers a solution by leveraging the computational resources of nearby devices to monitor vulnerable target units. However, this approach faces challenges when transferring models to constrained devices due to the computational overhead associated with traditional machine learning inference, a problem that is exacerbated further by the requirement to update models periodically with new features. This paper introduces "NBcoded," a novel tool designed to overcome these hurdles by compacting the Naive Bayes algorithm for efficient, periodic execution on low-power architecture. Developed using functional programming concepts to introduce a new training methodology for the algorithm, NBcoded also compacts both the algorithmic logic and associated data into two streamlined routines that together consume less than 10 KB of flash memory and operate within power devices. Empirical results demonstrate that NBcoded successfully detects approximately 85% of attack instances on these limited-resource devices while avoiding energy consumption during operation.

Video analysis offers a powerful avenue for examining human life, yet extracting meaningful data requires robust automation. While many such tasks have been well-studied for general motion, biological movement often holds the key to understanding life processes but has received considerably less attention. To address this, we first demonstrate how to distinguish biological from non-biological agents without relying on these common assumptions. Subsequently, we present a model capable of forecasting the trajectories of small biological entities—even when they are partially occluded—by exploiting patterns of cell-level internal activity.

Network power systems face increasing strain from renewable energy sources and electric vehicles, necessitating infrastructure upgrades. Tests conducted on various network instances demonstrate that our method surpasses both classical heuristic and, in many cases, non-hybrid VQE implementations. Additionally, the study highlights that non-hybrid VQE approaches struggle with convergence within reasonable time limits when employing realistic qubit count limitations.

The innovation here restructures the standard non-stochastic system into a stochastic one, allowing all model-related uncertainties to be incorporated into a dedicated drift term on the stochastic evolution. The estimates are then derived within a stochastic state-space framework, requiring the integration of measurements from distinct temporal layers. The related filtering problem comprises two components: high-frequency filtering, which processes individual video frames recorded at a fast rate, and low-frequency filtering, which works with measurement averages acquired at a slower pace. The performance limitations associated with multi-level filtering under different noise scenarios are examined, supported by numerical results from second-order simulation datasets. Furthermore, these numerical examples illustrate the utility of a new random variational approach for simultaneous state and parameter estimation, making it possible to estimate both object states and air resistance coefficients.

On-chip integrated quantum technologies rely heavily on advanced manufacturing techniques for various essential components, including waveguides, single-photon sources, and detectors. A critical milestone in this field is the development of an efficient platform for generating deterministic quantum light states, specifically at the single-photon level. Addressing this, we introduce and examine a novel design single-photon emitter featuring a Tapered waveguide section built into an aluminum nitride (AlN) microchip. This source operates via the spontaneous parametric down-conversion process. Our characterization reveals that the 200-microlong taper effectively boosts the collection of downloaded photons, a result supported by both experimental data and numerical simulations. Overall, this work presents a robust, scalable framework for generating entangled light beams and other complex quantum states on demand using on-chip integrated nonlinear photonic circuits.

Using Raman spectroscopy, we measured the damping of longitudinal acoustic waves in doped GaAs at low temperatures by analyzing their wavekeeper interactions. Our measurements reveal that at high temperatures, damping follows a $f^2$ law consistent with the soft potential model, whereas low-frequency behaviors diverge based on doping concentration. Specifically, undoped GaAs exhibits an approximately $f^{3/2}$-dependent damping, representing canonical behavior for the soft potential model, while heavily doped samples display $f^{3/2}$ scaling only above a distinct crossover frequency that varies with dopant level. Additionally, we observed that the envelope of the dispersed phonon mode narrows significantly over time in heavily doped GaAs. This prolongation suggests the emergence of non-Gaussian acoustic fluctuations in such materials, indicating complex local dynamical and spatial properties of lattice carriers in heavily doped GaAs.

We introduce a novel semi-numerical method designed to enhance—by orders of magnitude—the precision in achieving particle physics results that are semi-analytically derived. This formula-based strategy, known as "al algebraic numerical integration," blends calculus with computation to deliver—by several orders—enhanced accuracy. Numerous case studies confirm its versatility and precision upon which more rigorous theoretical and numerical efforts can be founded. We conclude by discussing prospective applications and directions for future endeavors in this manner.

We introduce simple approximations for a segment of an optical fiber that allow for the analytical derivation of the eigenchannels and their corresponding transmission matrix (TM). These eigenchannels describe the system's natural modes, while the TM characterizes average transmission from source to detector. By leveraging weakly perturbing LEDs, one can experimentally estimate and extract the actual transmission matrix. Furthermore, approximation models for higher-order modes based on a standard LED measurement enable the reconstruction of the system's junctions. The proposed approach is validated through both numerical simulations of a sp/splice connection and experimental results.

We present new observations of our central galaxy using the Submillimeter Array (sub-arcsecond resolution at 470 GHz / 0.64 millimeter wavelength), revealing the structure and kinematics of cold dust ($T \approx 30K$) through millimeter-wave data. This study identifies compelling evidence for a central milliparsec-scale bar, characterized by semi-amplitudes of 0.3–0.6 milliparsecs and a semi-axis range of 1.5–3 milliparsecs with orientations spanning from East-West to W-SW. Additionally, the analysis pinpoints dust knots exhibiting super-rotational velocities exceeding 10 micro-meters per second within areas smaller than one millisecond light-second, indicating significant turbulence. Furthermore, multiple co-localized velocity peaks suggest complex small-scale structures or overlying galactic discs. By simulating a pure-attractor model of a pure bar, this research establishes constraints on its parameters, defining the angular position around the East-West axis between East-West and W-SW, inclination angles ranging from 15/25 millisecond arcseconds, and width intervals from 15/25 millisecond arcseconds.

Multimodal optimization focuses on maximizing a single objective function while multi-objective optimization seeks a collection of compromise solutions, often visualized as a Pareto front, by balancing two or more conflicting objectives. Despite these differing goals, the two approaches maintain a critical connection: the two regions of the solution space can overlap, containing regions where multiple local optima co-exist. In the context of transformation between single- and multi-objective problems using local search, previous studies have identified three main evolutionary stages: the initial state with no front formation, the transitional phase, and the final state. While the first represents problem A and the third represents problem B (or vice versa), the second stage is key; the differences between the two problems manifest most distinctly during this intermediate transition phase, making it the primary subject of analysis. Existing techniques for converting between these formats generally fall into global strategies, local globalized approaches, or purely local methods. Prior work has evaluated global strategies and local globalized approaches; however, this study introduces and rigorously tests a local method that defines whether to treat the target as single-objective or multi-objective based purely on local information. By rigorously benchmarking this local method against existing globalized and global approaches using the Yallop benchmark suite—which features problems designed with specific dimensions and configurations that yield clear results—the research analyzes how the choice of transformation approach impacts algorithm performance. The findings demonstrate that utilizing local information is the superior choice, with the type of local method significantly influencing outcomes

Stable matchings identify mutually preferred pairs for binary valuations that maximize the sum of utilitarian welfare across all stable configurations. This study addresses binary valuations where the goal is a stable matching. It introduces a new stable matching concept for binary valuations maximizing utilitarian welfare and establishes two primary results. First, finding such a matching via the proposed definition, even with binary valuations tied to utilitarian welfare, is NP-hard, and no polynomial approximation exists unless P=N=P. Second, the paper presents an efficient algorithm to compute this stable matching with a linear time complexity, $O(n)$, again assuming binary valuations and the utilitarian objective. These conditions constitute necessary and sufficient constraints for computational efficiency. Additionally, the authors explore related stable matchings that ensure a minimally reduced utilitarian welfare loss, addressing the complexity of binary valuations related to utilitarian welfare. They also investigate other stable matchings utilizing utility ensembles for related complex parameters, specifically the utilitarian welfare and the egalitarian fairness.

Nonuniform strain induces both spontaneous valley Hall effects in pristine materials as well as anomalous valley Hall phenomena when paired with other forms of broken symmetries. While the first arises from real-space strain gradients, the second results from the hybridization of band states mediated by the strain-induced modification of atomic orbitals. This analysis investigates valley Hall transport in a generic low-symmetry atomically thin sheet utilizing a four-band model that elegantly unites models introduced by Baumbach et al. and Liu et al. Our findings indicate that a hole-doped $2D$ MoS₂ system exhibits substantial spontaneous valley Hall conductance in the vicinity of valley bands, with the capability of tuning this response through carrier doping. Conversely, in semimetals like MoSe₂ and WSe₂, both pristine and doped systems display an anomalous valley Hall effect where the Hall conductance can be adjusted via doping or strain engineering. Notably, the magnitudes predicted for these anomalous conductances exceed those of the spontaneous type. Beyond these effects, we uncover a novel mechanism wherein nonuniform strain triggers valley Hall conductance through the modulation of interband transition rates across the valley bands. Furthermore, we characterize a characteristic nonmonotonic dependence of valley Hall conductance on valley carrier density in such systems. Finally, we critically assess the experimental viability of observing these phenomena, emphasizing the significance of achieving low defect densities in moored 2D materials to validate these predictions.

Using the metrics of tiedness and convergence from metric spaces, we establish results regarding the centering of stabilizers in clouds that lack the traditional symmetry. Specifically, we prove a variant of Pitman–Blackwells theorem stating that any cluster of tuples with a nontrivial invariant group possesses at least one metric center point under specific conditions regarding uniform distribution over finite sets with trivial invariants against certain group actions. Furthermore, we demonstrate a strong connection between a center's stability and its radius—defined as the maximum distance from the cluster members—indicating that when the optimal radius remains bounded across a sequence of uniformly distributed clusters with consistently enlarged stabilizers, a subsequence must converge down the sequence of clusters using the tied topology for some central element within each component in that collection (of which there exists one suitable candidate). These theoretical findings have practical applications within automated group testing scenarios involving symmetric error patterns.

This paper introduces a circularly polarized dual-band microstrip antenna operating on frequency bands of 5.2 GHz and 5.6 GHz. The design utilizes an asymmetrically arranged single square element with a larger dimension on the left side to achieve the dual-band capability. By incorporating asymmetric feeding lines, the template is grounded, ensuring compliance with military handheld device form factors. The resulting dual-band operating mode exhibits superior characteristics, including a half-power beamwidth spanning 60 to 120 degrees, axial ratio less than than 3 dB across the matched bandwidth, and peak gain exceeding 5.5 dB. Furthermore, the proposed structure demonstrates robust robustness against polarization interference, satisfies standard electromagnetic compatibility norms regarding spurious emissions, and maintains compatibility with UWB channels by minimizing response in that frequency range.

Deciding upon quantum error correction strategies constitutes a core challenge in implementing practical quantum computers. We introduce a method grounded in reinforcement learning to tailor decoding approaches specifically for a given experimental setup, alongside theoretical validation of its efficacy. By leveraging machine learning techniques, we successfully fine-tune decoding policies on Google's Sycamore processor, achieving remarkable resilience against quantum error propagation during bit-flip error injection tests. Our successfully trained classifier effectively distinguishes genuine fault processes from injected artificial errors. Additionally, we present an automated, end-to-end framework that enables the rapid development and deployment of decoding strategies in response to evolving noise characteristics on the processor.

Quantum jumps enable the ultra-precise clocking of transitions between energy levels. By generalizing observations from a two-level system to scenarios with multiple levels, the authors introduce a broadened method known as quantum jump metrology. In specific instances, this approach achieves precision that surpasses traditional quantum fisher information limits. The authors demonstrate apply quantum jump methods to enhance the band structure detection from a three-level system. Additionally, they present a scheme for multiplying quantum numbers using entangled jumps, further proving the method's utility. These results establish quantum jump measurements as a potent instrument in the era of quantum technology, with significant potential for advancing measurements in both experimental and theoretical contexts.

This study introduces a novel approach to model the hadronization of jet-induced structures within jet-to-hadron correlations using a new formalism derived from color-coherent parton showers. By aligning this modeling strategy with recent LHCmC data across multiple observables spanning both low and high $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ ranges in Au+Au collisions, we assess the power distribution of hadrons across the kinematic spectrum of $\mathrm{Au+Au}$ collisions, leveraging an established LHCmC framework. Results indicate that the yield of hadrons from this source decreases substantially as the quark's longitudinal momentum fraction ($z$) diminishes. Furthermore, we quantify enhancements in jet activity attributed to LHCmC conditions relative to $pp$ collisions, achieving peak ratios of approximately five times for $10 < \mathrm{GeV} < \mathrm{GeV}$.

The digital-analog framework for quantum computation facilitates a range of tasks, including the simulation of many-body systems and algorithms like Grover's search. Focusing on digital-analog Grover's algorithm, we analyze conditions under which it can effectively locate loaded states in a Fermi-Hubbard model on a two-dimensional lattice, even in the presence of noise. We find that, unlike other models, this algorithm's performance is only marginally affected by noise. Furthermore, we investigate how trapped ion systems can physically realize Fermi-Hubbard modeling through this approach, analyzing error sources in trapped ion qubits. Finally, we estimate the number of qubits and circuit cycles needed to achieve meaningful state preparation, suggesting that existing experimental setups in trapped ions are well-positioned to demonstrate this protocol soon.

Bonsai is an automated algorithm designed to feature-engineer input data into richer representations suitable for subsequent machine learning models. It builds features using linear combinations and nonlinear transformations (such as trigonometric and logarithmic operations), or by training lightweight "mini-models" on residual errors to capture unlearned patterns, mimicking the approach of single-layer and multi-layer neural networks. Guided by modern neural search techniques known as reinforcement learning with policies, Bonsai performs hierarchical feature construction and has been validated against the traditional hand-engineering process across three real-world datasets: LandUse, Quid, and CQA. Validation included comparison with neural networks benchmarking the transformed data, demonstrating Bonsai's ability to build diverse and effective representations. Manual inspection confirmed the generated features are diverse and meaningful. Ultimately, both Bonsai-transformed data and comparable single-layer models outperformed existing models within all data sets used in this study.

This study introduces a weighted-mutation assisted genetic algorithm capable of achieving both high resolution and contrast contrast in scattering media. By incorporating a proposed fuzzy model, the method determines optimal weights for scattered light, enabling the identification of a unique light source with point-to-point mapping even within scattering environments. While effectively enhancing scattering media characterization, this approach also demonstrates its versatility by applying to other inverse problems involving photon transport phenomena, particularly in deep tissue imaging contexts where enhanced imaging qualities rely on improved image clarity and detail.

Recent efforts aimed at reducing the sample complexity of policy evaluation have relied heavily on sampling state transitions specifically from estimated posterior distributions over unvisited state transitions derived during data collection. This paper offers a theoretical analysis of these efficient estimation methods for their sample efficiency. We demonstrate that even when these posterior distributions are accurately reconstructed, the testing sample size determines sample efficiency rather than the accuracy of the underlying underlying state reachability or posterior estimates. Based on this insight, we propose a novel efficient value function estimator that includes a confidence interval, achieving significant performance with both fewer samples and less computational effort compared to prior approaches. Furthermore, we validate these theoretical claims through simulations and clarify them empirically using real-world robotics data.

Monolithic small-charge-collector (SCE) CMOS sensors utilize high-voltage p-type CMOS chips, where a robust thick high-resistivity silicon substrate serves as the large-volume sensor, while a thin layer of n-type doping under each small charge-collection electrode minimizes inherent capacitance. Although these robust sensors effectively reject particles and possess strong positioning accuracy even at high radiation flux and elevated operating temperatures, improving the timing resolution in SCE sensors remains a key hurdle. In this paper, we conducted simulations using the standard SCE sensor design, employing the TCAD tool to analyze various structural configurations, particularly focusing on reducing total sensor-layer thickness. Thinner structures were found to enhance total resistivity, which significantly improves charge-dispersion and total resistivity. In reduced configurations, the bulk resistivity increases, reducing carrier dispersion; this improvement in total resistivity, the charging time and resistivity were significantly better. We introduce Planetary Agnostic NEBula Removal Algorithm (PANRNA), a new technique designed to remove sky neonluus (NEB) from ground-based imaging without needing a reference template. Reducing NEBs is critical for extending exoplanet hunting capabilities in current observing programs, as these bright artifacts often obscure faint companions. While existing methods often rely on template matching—which demands a reference template and risks propagating its flaws—or complex, computation-heavy machine learning approaches that analyze individual science frames (and further spread artifacts if the template is imperfect)—PANRNA offers an intermediate solution. By applying an unsupervised, template-free scheme to this problem, the method successfully isolates and remove NEBs directly from the data in real time. We demonstrate its efficacy using Hubble Space Telescope (HST) data (where NEBs are absent) to validate that our procedure leaves science signals largely untouched and achieves significant extenuation of visible planets mimicking true exoplanets within simulated high-contrast environments. Ultimately, we show using both simulations and observations that PANRNA successfully extends the detectable limit down to approximately 6.5 magnitudes in contrast for a 0.2" separation.

This study introduces a model for forecasting Italian regional interest rates characterized by its capacity to incorporate complex data sources—including textual data under normal market conditions and negative interest rates during exceptional periods—without imposing mathematical constraints on input variables. Achieved through a fully Bayesian framework integrated with a spatial random effect and a restrictive network prior, this model addresses the mathematical challenges of conventional approaches. Furthermore, predictive efficacy is significantly enhanced by accounting for temporal correlation among regions. The findings demonstrate both the improved predictive performance relative to standard methodologies and the model's capacity to identify exceptional periods distinct from typical market behavior.

Although no evidence for sterile neutrinos has emerged to date, the DUNE collaboration's long-range project retains a viable search capability for such entities via its Near Detector (NDA). Our study evaluates how the ND configuration specifically influences the potential to detect sterile neutrinos, noting that existing formal documentation for the ND is absent. An approximate ND geometry was therefore constructed to function as a rapid simulation wrapper based on GEANT4, facilitating full macro files for complete, high-speed simulations within Scintillating Liquid Argon (LArAPS). These accelerated simulations were executed using ProLato workloads for a population study of selected event variables across multiple scenarios. The findings indicate that utilizing the LArAPS near-ND simulation wrapper allows for a thorough investigation of its performance within the DUNE environment and suggests the system is well-suited for full simulation requirements, provided an approximate ND model incorporating lead structures and support wiring is employed.

Building upon established techniques for adjusting p-values and confidence intervals for cluster-robust inference, we introduce two novel cluster-robust estimators that enhance the precision of these adjustments, particularly for samples with limited cluster counts. The first method, an **empirical Bayes approach**, utilizes a flexible empirical prior derived from p-values, alongside derived formulas for asymptotic uncertainty. The second approach employs a **local Gaussian copula** based on multivariate structure. Both methods offer analytical assessments of asymptotic variance. We demonstrate, through simulations that the proposed estimators yield superior first-order accuracy compared to the standard Bonferroni procedure and competitive second-order accuracy relative to the Canfield and Bondell method. Finally, real-world adjustments to two commonly used policies using new estimation techniques confirm that the proposed approaches yield substantial gains.

In computational fluid dynamics, numerical methods for particle-laden flows often suffer when the growth in particle mass significantly decouples the time-step limitations found in empty-domain solvers. We introduce the Multiple-Time-Step Integration Algorithm (MTSA) (also known as the multiple-time-step algorithm, whose traditional implementation via subcycling typically requires particle trajectories to be tracked within the coarser time-step framework), which allows the time-step for particle trajectory tracking to be independently coarsened via trajectory coarsening. During testing, this new algorithm proved advantageous in two key areas by increasing the size of the time-step without altering other parameters and actually decreasing the size of the time-step required to simulate a given physical scenario, with performance measured relative to the standard single-time-step approach used for all components. The algorithm's accuracy was validated against existing methods using two benchmark cases: a dense particle-laden Taylor-Green vortex flow and a particle-laden channel with periodic step-hindrance, whose results showed excellent consistency with prior studies and demonstrated high fidelity. Furthermore, the method exhibits robust scalability in both computational domains (the size of fluid grid points) and particle scaling (the number of moving particles), making it well-suited for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles on modern high-performance computing architectures that utilize massive processor counts. We demonstrate that for an observer situated outside a black hole, particle number emerges as the primary definition of number density when measured by the local proper energy, with numbers infinite in the local proper time. This concept aligns with findings from classical general rel theories showing that black hole evaporation arises because the vacuum state transforms into other states upon translation along the local proper time direction; importantly, we clarify on exactly what states the evaporation occurs. Furthermore, our research reveals that black hole evaporation can be comprehended as the transformation of vacuum states without requiring any modification to quantum field theory on curved spacetime. The methodology employed is numbers operator on local proper time directions for particles locally measured by such observers. Utilizing this operator, our framework resolves fundamental ambiguities regarding the definition of particle number for the local proper time directions and clarifies the physical conditions under which black hole evaporation arises. Additionally, our formulation elucidates the nature of information storage within evaporating black holes. Although these results have been derived for non-extremal, spherically non-extremal black holes, the mathematical operator methodology is universally applicable to all forms of particle number definitions across various theoretical scenarios.

This study presents an examination of nuclear broadening $\langle q_t^2 \rangle$ within the framework of the color evaporation model, specifically at the LHC. Because this quantity depends on the dipole cross section $\sigma(\mathbf{r\,)}$, we evaluated $\langle q_t^2 \rangle$ using three distinct theoretical models for $\sigma(\mathbf{r\,)}$: the color transparency (CT) model, the color transparency with LHC parameters (CT-LHC), and the multiple scattering (MS) approach. Our calculated results align well with experimental $\langle q_t^2 \rangle$ values from RHIC and $\langle P_{t}^{2}\rangle$ measurements from the LHC. Furthermore, we extended these calculations to predict broadening for various systems and centrality configurations at L energies, comparing the outcomes with available data. Using the defined models, we further analyzed nuclear $W^+$ production and found that the shape of the rapidity and transverse-momentum distributions remains consistent across CT, CT-LHC, and MS frameworks, whereas the cross-section magnitude varies significantly, prompting a preference for the CT model in $W$-boson calculations. Finally, the study addressed small-$x$ physics by calculating nuclear structure functions $F_2(x,Q^2)$ and longitudinal structure function terms $F_L(x,Q^2)$ within the low-$x$ framework.

A numerical analysis was conducted to examine the dynamics of a two-dimensional liquid channel entraining air. The numerical model was validated against previously reported experimental findings by Lim et al. (2009) and the theoretical analyses provided by Lim et al. The results demonstrate that the entrained air influences the stability of the downstream liquid tail as well as the overall stability of the interface. Furthermore, the predictions align with experimental observations showing a strong correlation between the stability of the interface and the jet's tail. The study identifies that unsteady phenomena arise due to the penetration of air bubbles into the thick folds of the interface and the subsequent shedding of these structures. The research suggests that while entrapped air contributes significantly to the complex dynamics of liquid channels, it is not the sole factor responsible for the generation of such irregular flow patterns.

Modern applications leveraging Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) rely extensively on software frameworks and libraries to exploit new hardware capabilities. A critical concern for transactional programs using NVM is guaranteeing data consistency during system crashes and power failures while avoiding expensive barrier operations in normal operation to maintain performance. Although existing technique often ensures data consistency by relying exclusively on in-memory logging or record logging—both of which necessitate hardware support—we introduce a flexible, algorithm-driven approach that maintains data durability through consistent data validation and undo capabilities stored on stable storage (non-volatile backing store) without requiring logarithmic protocols or additional barrier instructions. Our methods have been integrated into full-scale key-value and document key-value applications and executed on leading commercial NVM platforms (Intel Optane and Samsung NVMe SSDs with OpEnCL). Evaluation results across varied workloads reveal significant enhancements in both throughputs and latitudes when employing our proposed unwinding strategies, with performance that is algorithm-only based rather than relying solely on traditional logging approaches; besides this performance gain it provides lower overhead full scalability operating without requiring logging based systems that currently limit commercial availability.

The Hierarchy Document Topic Model (HDTM) is a statistical method designed to analyze the structure of information networks by grouping them into clusters and sub-clusters based on content-based similarity. By operating at an abstract level using metadata—enabling analysis of diverse networks from social media to legal and political domains where direct access to actual links is impossible—HDTM has proven effective. However, interpreting this multi-level output remains difficult. To address this, we introduce an agnostic visualization technique that operates independent of the specific underlying algorithm but capitalizes at its results. Specifically designed for HDTM outputs, we develop a hypergraph-based layout method that produces force-directed visualizations. Combined with an interactive 3D d3.js visualization interface, this approach facilitates detailed exploratory analysis, allowing users to identify community patterns and understand both global network traits and local document-level dynamics. Demonstrated specifically with the interactive visualization of the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election information space, the tool yields significant insights into dominant narrative patterns and individual network positions.

This study examines three-body systems initialized within a confined spatial volume, focusing specifically on two-dimensional configurations. We analyze two distinct initial velocity assignment schemes: a uniform random distribution and a normal random distribution, alongside an assessment of three key statistical metrics—escape time, final bound mass ratio (for cases where no body escapes immediately), and pre-escape pericenter distance of the separating chunk. We contrast our findings with existing predictions made by Chai et al. (2007), discovering excellent agreement on pericenter distance and final mass ratios for both schemes. However, a significant divergence arises with respect to initial conditions: theoretical models accurately anticipated trends in escape time under uniform random distributions but failed to do so for normal random distributions. To investigate the pericenter-conditional escape time distribution, we conducted Monte Carlo simulations on simulation sets partitioned pericenter and discovered that, under uniformly random velocity initialization, escape would soon occur following a pericenter minimum, whereas normal random initial velocities result in a substantially delayed separation process. Finally, we present theoretical formulas intended to accurately forecast three-body dynamical interactions under normal random initial velocity conditions.

The ALICE collaboration at the LHC reported recently on the observation of $\text{psi}(2S)$ mesons within proton-proton (pp) collisions occurring at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Specifically, this note investigates the suppression of these mesons across varying multiparticle densities in proton-lead (p-Pb) collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\text{NN}}}=5.04$ TeV, contrasting the findings with previous results derived from collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\text{NN}}}=2.78$ TeV. By comparing with data gathered under the same multiparticle density conditions but via superposition models, we have assessed the degree of suppression experienced by $\text{psi}(2S)$ mesons relative to those of J/$\text{psi}$ mesons. Our analysis indicates that while both species exhibit similar suppression trends up to a certain threshold of transverse momentum ($p_{\text{T}} \approx 10$ GeV/c), p-Pb collisions result in noticeably less suppression (a anti-suppression effect) for $\text{psi}(2S)$ mesons compared to J/$\text{psi}$ mesons when the transverse momentum exceeds 10 GeV/c. Furthermore, this note offers a preliminary examination of potential modifications in the yield ratios of $\text{psi}(2S)$ to excited B mesons under both pp and heavy-ion collision environments.

For any countable language, we suggest a force axiom schema denoted as $E$, whose applications address Tarski's finite-to-one extension theorem and the continuum hypothesis within continuous first-order logic. Using this framework, we demonstrate that any countable structure can be expanded to a generic model for the countable force axms $E$ in the language it generates. Furthermore, we prove the continuous first-order continuous Tarski's finite-to-one extension theorem and show that the existence of uncountable cardinality can be proved in the continuous first-order logic using only axms. Specifically, we propose the axiom E as a force axiom for each countable logic. Finally, we utilize continuous first-order logic to prove the continuum hypothesis, extending it in the sense of Tarski's finite-to-one extension theorem.

Sequential attention mechanisms have proven beneficial for deep sequential modeling, addressing limitations like error accumulation over long inputs and making latent states explicit via attenuation. This work introduces a new adaptive attention scheme designed to automatically align specific temporal ranges, such as time ranges in climate data. We illustrate its application within an adaptive Range-aware Time-series Transformer (RTTN) model, demonstrating that our approach surpasses contemporary baselines—including Transformers, LSTMs, and Temporal Convolutional Networks—across univariate and multivariate forecasting tasks. Furthermore, the proposed learning algorithm is capable of explicitly identifying relevance ranges for a given dataset to explain predictive decisions. The effectiveness of this approach was validated on extensive datasets, such as M4/MTM, with additional insights provided for synthetic and noisy datasets. Finally, all model implementations, experimental data, and results are accessible at https://github.com/mauro-ferretti/adaptive_range_transformer.

Dense quark matter exists within the interior of quark stars, and it is likely organized into distinct phases near the center, with phases like the color-flavor locked (CFL) superconducting state potentially occupying such a structure. A critical feature distinguishing these systems is the capacity for phase boundaries, particularly separating CFL matter from normal matter, to create discontinuities in energy density that cause a matter transition and resulting density jump. This work examines quark stars comprising a CFL core encased by layers of dense normal quark matter, applying a piecewise polytropic equation of state to model star profiles under various scenarios. By analyzing the differential behavior of mass and radius across the parameter space of the piecewise polynomial state of state, we identify signatures indicating a discontinuous phase transition versus a smooth phase transition.

This research examines warp morphologies across 50 late-type galaxy systems, analyzing their structural parameters and structural index (WI) against the galaxies' specific energy density profiles derived from environment. Using WI measurements from external photometric data and the Dehlinger model, we found strong correlations for both S-type and U-type warped galaxies while determining that U-type warped systems exhibit a higher structural index. These findings indicate that S-type systems possess a more mature evolution than their U-type counterparts. Furthermore, an analysis of the environments surrounding these galaxies using the two-point correlation function (2PCF) and the Tidal Disruption Radius (TDR) revealed distinct influence patterns. For S-type systems, environment plays a more direct role in formation, characterized by higher specific energy density, weaker tidal repercussions, and a reduced likelihood of interactions with a TDR-limited neighboring galaxy, suggesting a more selective formation process. Conversely, the formation and evolution of U-type warped systems are more comprehensively dictated by their broader galactic milieu; this is characterized by stronger tidal effects and more diverse TDR scenarios, implying their creation involves a wider array of interactions with nearby galaxies within their disruption radius. Ultimately, our study demonstrates a robust correlation between the WI and a galaxy's specific energy density in both categories, leading to the conclusion that increasing morphological complexity correlates with decreasing structural stability across both S-type and U-type warped galaxies.

We analyze a third-order differential inequality observed by D. Zhang specifically regarding harmonic functions on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons. This demonstrates that if harmonic functions satisfying a specific sub-exponential growth condition are limited to a dimensionality no greater than $ \frac{3}{2} $, then such functions must be constant. Relational models achieve significant success in pharmacology through their capacity to encode and utilize structural knowledge within chemical datasets. However, the literature for these models frequently employs different benchmarking strategies for comparison. Adopting mixed evaluation methods hinders meaningful contrast between competing technologies and limits reasonable estimates of error margins. Consequently, we introduce Pharmacological Relational Models Zoo (PRZ), the initial comprehensive benchmarking framework for diverse relational systems applied to pharmacological tasks. PRZ compares thirteen distinct relational models across four datasets by standardizing metrics such as latency, training stability, and test accuracy to promote equitable comparisons. Our analysis reveals no single dominant system; instead, performance varies by task and dataset, with only two models demonstrating consistent leadership. These findings further highlight the inherent uncertainty in relational modeling outcomes, suggesting that reported literature results should be interpreted as approximate ranges rather than fixed figures. Ultimately, PRZ aims to guide the evolution of relational modeling in pharmacology by establishing robust, standardized benchmarks for future research.

Neural networks have emerged as a powerful approach for resolving inverse problems that are often ill-posed and lack well-defined analytical solutions. Existing methodologies typically involve training networks using synthetic data pairs, pairing measured inputs with known ground truth for the corresponding source problems. Consequently, a critical research challenge is leveraging neural networks for inverse problem solving without access to labeled ground truth. Address this gap, we present a novel algorithm that employs neural networks as a proxy for direct-posed problem resolution. This framework utilizes a neural network-trained estimator to transform the inverse problem into a constrained optimization task through a weak first-order approximation. We further introduce practical, data-free protocols for incorporating prior knowledge on the inputs. By merging these elements, we formulate a proximal-type iterative algorithm that iteratively refines estimates by alternating between optimizing a proxy loss function and project steps informed by these prior constraints. Remarkably, despite the introduction of network approximations and linearized constraints, theoretical analysis demonstrates that our proposed method remains rigorously correct for the original problems. Valid through extensive experiments on both synthetic datasets and sources including the Rock-and-Roll Collection and Nasa's Space Radiation Database, results confirm that this technique effectively addresses scenarios where ground truth is unavailable.

The option paradigm offers a system-level mechanism for managing system-wide configurations, with millions of software systems employing runs-time options to enhance compatibility, ensure backward compatibility, and support gradual paradigm shifts. While previous research has highlighted the benefits of option usage, the risks associated with this paradigm remain under-explored. We introduce a static analysis technique designed to identify such redundant options by aggregating software call graphs and control flow graphs to establish reachability without incurring the overheads typically associated with instrumentalizing code executions. Empirical evaluations on real-world software reveal that this approach accurately detects a significant quantity of these anomalies. Furthermore, we present a strategy to quantitatively reduce binary sizes by eliminating these dormant options. Ultimately, the findings suggest a path forward: by detecting these unused options early in the development lifecycle, developers can address the resulting bloat proactively.

Quantum teleportation stands as one of quantum information theory's most compelling concepts, enabling the transfer of entangled quantum states between distant locations through local quantum operations and the shared distribution of entangled qubits. Although theoretically established since its inception, experimental realizations of teleportation have historically struggled with low fidelity due to challenges in generating high-purity, entangled pairs of exciton-polariton states. This work demonstrates quantum teleportation utilizing anti-polariton qubits, a system known for producing on-demand entangled pairs via Kerr-nonlinear interactions that circumvent many typical purity issues. Specifically, we achieve a fidelity of $F=0.693 \pm 0.0753$ at a rate of $1.04 \times 10^4$ Hz with an indistinguishability parameter of $0.63 \pm 0.08$ for both polarizations, achieving a significant advancement over previous achievements. This breakthrough highlights the potential of anti-polariton systems for developing advanced quantum information processing technologies.

These inputs feed into the CNN for IBI estimation, with WPM loss addressing amplitude discrepancies between predicted and true values. During testing, traditional time algorithms process our outputs to generate the final result: we compare four deep-learning architectures using synthetic datasets featuring various noise levels. Using open-access sets with real-world noisy data from actual patients, we evaluate accuracy via the Concordance Correlation Coefficient.
