Recent investigations into Brownian motion driven by active forces have demonstrated that, unlike thermal systems, fluctuations in such active scenarios differ significantly at large scales. This study examines the dynamics of a Brownian particle influenced by an arbitrary time-dependent, stationary random force. It is established that variations in time across a broad spectrum—from high to low frequencies—follow a log-normal distribution regardless of the magnitude of the control parameters, including particle size, viscosity, and force intensity. Moreover, unlike the Gaussian fluctuations typical of thermal fluctuations at large scales, fluctuations induced by active forces conform to skew-Levy distributions with a scaling exponent of 3/2 at low frequencies or, equivalently, a high-frequency cutoff characterized by a fractional derivative operator with order less than or equal to 3/2. These analytical predictions are supported by Monte Carlo simulations of a specific model, the Harmonic Random Accelerator (HRA). Remarkably, despite anharmonic random accelerators exhibiting different microscopic properties, they produce nearly identical macroscopic behavior.

We introduce a new methodology for achieving more photorealistic 3D modeling of human emotional expressions by utilizing historical modeling data to fill gaps. To develop this method, we created HUMBI, a framework capable of compressing diverse expression styles from a training set of face models into compressed historical latent parameters for future synthetic generative tasks. Extensive tests on novel audio samples demonstrate that our method produces high-quality facial animations with realistic physical details.

The underlying algebraic and topological structure of these Markovian models is established, with particular emphasis on the computation of invariant subspaces relative to the action of the group derived from a dynamical system. This paper investigates the relative $I$-functions associated with toric complete intersections, even when smoothness conditions are absent. It establishes an identity linking the $I$-function derived from the ambient space to that of the complete intersection via a finite relation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, under specific circumstances, proving the cremer-cremer statement for toric variations reduces to verifying a collection of recurrence relations.

This study introduces an approximate complete transmission framework for linear piezoelectric materials under frequency-domain conditions, specifically where the wavelength is significantly smaller than the thickness of the model domain. The core of this transmission approach expresses the surface fields on one side as functions of adjacent surface fields, utilizing an asymptotic expansion based on piezoelectric homogenization of the internal state. This singular interface condition enables efficient cross-coupling of computational paths for piezoelectric materials with distinct characteristics, eliminating the need to explicitly represent electromagnetic fields with varying transverse resolutions in numerical simulations. Consequently, this significantly abates memory requirements when utilizing standard finite element methods across patches with thicknesses differing by an order of magnitude, as demonstrated by numerical examples for standard piezoelectric crystals like PZT and ZnO.

Leaving the material specifics aside, we outline a general theoretical approach for spatial light modulation within an optical framework describing matter-light interaction. This methodology accounts immediately from the start for the feedback loop created by traveling matter waves. By generalizing the Keldysh non-linear $\sigma$-model to incorporate polariton condensates under spatial translation, we demonstrate that phase and amplitude control within this condensed phase can be achieved through the modulation of input light. Our findings specifically highlight that using vortex beams yields a condensed vortex state, while optical solitons—created via transverse standing waves—manifest as a dual-mode state Higgs-beam. These results are harnessed to propose techniques that probe loss mechanisms, including Higgs-mode excited states for examining non-equilibrium dynamics and spatially sustained period-doubling oscillations driven by counteracting gain and loss. Although these concepts apply broadly, we validate their distinct contributions specifically within a Higgs-basis Ginzburg-Landau framework.

The planet K2-22 b, confirmed by the Keck I/II ENAMINE spectrographs to harbor an atmosphere rich in CO2 with potential H2O, is a world of 1.7 Earth-masses orbiting a solar-like star (G1V) at a distance of 0.06 AU. Its equilibrium temperature stands at 380 K, leading many to view it as a "sub-Neptune" capable of retaining its primordial H/He envelope; its exact mass places it on the boundary between such an envelope and a purely rocky composition. This study employs the energy-limited mass loss equation to determine the planet's atmospheric depletion timescale. We utilized OpenSource tools (BATMAN and PyEPSILON) to refine the transit data provided by the NASA Keck I LDRR spectrographs. Our analysis reveals the presence of water vapor through a clear 1.4 μm absorption line. Using the measured enhancement of CO2 relative to this line to derive the molecular density, we estimated the mass loss rate to be approximately $6.8 \times 10^{-21}$ kg/s. Assuming the loss rate remains constant, we calculate an atmospheric lifetime of roughly 1.7 GY. Finally, we discuss how these results constrain models regarding the planet's current state and its evolution.

Building on a theorem of Stillman and Ye, we organize the space of homogeneous polynomials based on the fiber-diffeomorphism type of their associated Milnor fibration. This classification yields an algorithm that determines, for any given polynomial, the topological equivalence class of its Milnor fibration. Furthermore, our framework generalizes and refines prior results by CNF Chen and D. R. Peters regarding the space of non-degenerate polynomials.

A common data structure in analytics is the sparse array, which stores operations solely on nonzero values; both the C++ Armadillo and Python Scipy libraries utilize implementations that support efficient mathematical operations on these arrays. Yet, programming these specific configurations—such as sparse dimensions and size constraints—poses challenges when using their generic syntax. This code requires defining complex SFINAE or user-provided type traits within generic functions, leading to difficulties in type checking and maintenance. In contrast, this paper introduces a solution by enabling such type-safe operations directly through standard Python typing modules without needing advanced features like SFINAE or custom traits. This approach was achieved by developing fully recursive Generic Type Families using these standard type tools.

Although Galileo is celebrated as the founder of the empirical scientific method, his actual body of work often falls short of truly empirical standards; accordingly, his physical descriptions sometimes lack observation-based validation while his mathematical derivations rely on logically or historically prior assumptions that require reconsideration. Specifically, while Galileo's first law of motion is historically linked to his principle of inertia, the latter was actually shaped by the thoughts of his predecessors, making it unclear how much based on it was genuinely observed. Similarly, although his laws of free fall and compound motion are famous, their early demonstrations were not rigorously tested until the advent of modern timing instruments like electric circuits and light gates; even subsequent attempts at demonstration—such as those found in his book Two New Messages—are riddled with historical and logical errors. Consequently, rather than being strictly observed, these core principles should be understood as outcomes of flawed but resourceful approximations. This analysis highlights German physicist Philipp von Jolly's later contributions as a model for rigorously validating Galileo's original claims.

To bridge macroscopic magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and local kinetic physics, we developed a 2D asymptotic expansion model based on a modified Grad-Shafranov equation for the current profile, coupled with a differential equation governing magnetic stream function perturbations. These coupled equations encapsulate both global MHD forces and local phenomena such as magnetic reconnection within isolated islands. By applying a coordinate transformation to singularly handle interaction regions formed when magnetic islands coalesce, we established a modified approach that remains valid near these areas. Analytical solutions were derived for various configurations of two- and three-island interactions. Results indicate that nonlinear effects substantially alter magnetic field structures and broaden the operational parameter space for asymptotic expansion by accurately capturing island coalescence. Furthermore, we validated this extended model against standard Stochastic Field (SFEL) codes and 2D resistive magnetohydrodynamics simulations. The agreement between predictions and these numerical simulations across diverse scenarios reinforces the robustness of the Stochastic Field Law application in capturing magnetic island coalescence while maintaining consistency with numerical solutions.

How do digital helpers like chat agents form long-term plans? As collaborative tools, they eventually require the ability to construct complex strategies grounded in implicit world knowledge. Unlike current methodical policy frameworks that depend on explicit state transitions or simple action histories, this paper explores how agents can infer implicit world dynamics from their interaction history. Specifically, it introduces a novel framework enabling joint learning between policy and a memory mechanism that constructs structured world models. Central to our approach is the development of recurrent neural network-based semantic actions, performed by the agent for the purpose of communication with human partners. These semantic actions are designed for the task of structure preservation; thus they serve as abstract concepts capable of encapsulating multiple concrete actions taken during the task execution over time. Through the systematic integration these semantic concepts into shared interactions, the model's ability to learn compact, explicit world dynamics and explainable actions is also increased. In turn it can also support of how multi-step actions are selected based upon the current world model for the purpose promoting effective co-operative behavior between humans and machines.
